synopsis: This theoretical paper separates what a controller can represent from what observational demonstrations identify. It proves that distribution-preserving future-then-action imitation recovers the same population action conditional as behavior cloning. An exact world-action joint can nevertheless support planning when action effects are identified and candidate actions are explicitly conditioned upon. A deterministic example establishes an information advantage from intervention; it is a mathematical construction, not an empirical robotics result. [E07, E08, E13, E14, E17]

problem.text: Does predicting a future before inferring an action confer stronger control capability when both learners receive the same demonstrations? The paper distinguishes external policy expressivity, population training targets, and identification of alternative action consequences, leaving finite-sample learning performance outside its main analysis.

contributions.text: The paper establishes unrestricted controller-class equivalence through marginalization, then separately proves equality of observational imitation targets. Reproducing the demonstrator's complete trajectory distribution additionally requires behavior sufficiency.

It distinguishes information in the future predictor from information in the complete future-action joint. The former has an irreducible action-specific prediction gap; the latter can recover supported observational forward conditionals, with causal interpretation requiring further assumptions.

It constructs observationally indistinguishable environments with different optimal actions, proving a regret separation between observational and interventional learners rather than between unrestricted policy architectures.

The author argues that future supervision and video pretraining can still improve practical learning despite population equivalence. These proposed benefits are compatible with the theory but are not quantified empirically here.

inputs: Common deployment history H, containing goal/context, observations, and past actions. [E03]
Observational tuples (H, A, Y), where the recorded future Y is unavailable at action-selection time. [E03]
For control optimization: a known utility and an identified action-conditioned outcome or next-history kernel. Interventional learners additionally receive intervention outcomes. [E03, E06]
outputs: A stochastic history-to-action policy and its induced closed-loop trajectory distribution. [E03, E07]
Theoretical equivalence, prediction-error, identification, and regret statements; no trained neural controller is specified. [E07–E09, E12–E18]

steps.name: Define the comparison through observable behavior
steps.detail: The environment is a finite-horizon partially observed process. Capability classes group policies by their induced trajectory distributions across an environment family. Controller classes specify representable behavior; learner classes specify information available for choosing a controller.

steps.name: Factor the observational joint
steps.detail: Behavior cloning predicts A from H. World-action imitation fits q_F(Y|H) and q_I(A|H,Y). The factorization also permits a single network inducing these conditionals; it does not require two separate networks. The inverse conditional is a behavior posterior, retaining the demonstrator's action prior.

steps.name: Recover and identify a forward conditional
steps.detail: Normalize the exact joint at a specified action to obtain p_mu(Y|H,A). Positive action support makes this normalization possible. Consistency and conditional exchangeability, together with positivity, identify it with the interventional outcome kernel.

steps.name: Compare consequences under a utility
steps.detail: An identified outcome model supports one-step expected-utility maximization. For sequential planning, the framework instead uses a controlled next-history kernel to generate policy-dependent rollouts and optimize a trajectory utility.

training.text: The observational objectives are expected negative log likelihoods under the true demonstration distribution. Their exact minimizers recover p_mu(A|H), p_mu(Y|H), and p_mu(A|H,Y), assuming realizability and global population optimization.

This is an idealized learning comparison: future labels come from the same trajectories, and the equivalence assumptions remove estimation, approximation, and optimization errors. No neural training stages, frozen modules, or compute budget are instantiated.

inference.text: Standard world-action deployment samples a future and its conditional action, or exactly marginalizes the future. Its executed action distribution is the resulting marginal. MAP decoding, verifier selection, or temperature changes can alter that marginal while leaving the controller flattenable.

Planning explicitly fixes each candidate action, evaluates its predicted consequences, and selects by utility. Predicted outcomes are internal calculations; the environment evolves after the selected action is executed. Exact sequential optimality requires model correctness on every history-action pair reachable by candidate policies.

equations.expression: L_A = E_{p_mu}[-log pi_A(A|H)]; L_WA = E_{p_mu}[-log q_F(Y|H) - log q_I(A|H,Y)].
equations.explanation: The two population objectives fit an action conditional and a future-action joint, respectively. Their expectations concern the true demonstration distribution, not a finite training sample.

equations.expression: pi_WA(a|h) = integral q_F(y|h) q_I(a|h,y) dy; at the population optimum, pi_WA*(a|h) = p_mu(a|h) = pi_A*(a|h).
equations.explanation: Marginalizing the exact observational joint removes the future variable. Equality holds almost everywhere under demonstration histories; behavior sufficiency supplies the additional link to demonstrator trajectory equality.

equations.expression: T_q^WA(y|h,a) = q_F*(y|h) q_I*(a|h,y) / sum_{y'} q_F*(y'|h) q_I*(a|h,y').
equations.explanation: For a positive denominator, this is p_mu(y|h,a). It equals T_a(y|h) = P(Y=y|H=h,do(A=a)) only under the stated causal identification conditions. Using this conditional differs from marginalizing to imitate.

equations.expression: E_int(q_g) = I_int_{nu,rho}(A;Y|H) + E_{H~nu}[D_KL(T_rho(.|H) || g(.|H))], where T_rho = sum_a rho(a|H) T_a.
equations.explanation: Here nu evaluates histories, rho selects candidate actions, and g ignores the current candidate action. Its best achievable interventional KL risk is the action-outcome mutual information under this evaluation distribution.

results.setting: Realizable exact observational objectives, common deployment information, distribution-preserving deployment, and behavior sufficiency; no empirical dataset or split.
results.metric: Decision-complete control distance, equal to trajectory total variation
results.comparison: Both policies also induce the demonstrator's trajectory distribution under behavior sufficiency.
results.interpretation: No bounded trajectory utility distinguishes these ideal policies. This does not establish equality between particular finite neural implementations.

results.setting: Uniform future, inverse-action, and direct-action TV bounds over every history reachable by either compared policy.
results.metric: Trajectory total variation over horizon T
results.value: Proved upper bound: 1 - (1 - epsilon)^T <= T epsilon, with epsilon = min{1, epsilon_F + epsilon_I + epsilon_A}.
results.comparison: The corresponding per-history action TV distance is at most epsilon.
results.interpretation: This is a conditional continuity bound, not a measured error or a sample-complexity guarantee.

results.setting: Candidate actions sampled from rho at histories sampled from nu; the compared future predictor ignores the current candidate action.
results.value: Proved minimum for the action-unconditioned predictor: I_int_{nu,rho}(A;Y|H).
results.comparison: An exact action-conditioned kernel has zero risk.
results.interpretation: The gap is positive when supported candidate actions have differing outcome distributions on a positive-measure history set. It concerns prediction, and applies to the future component rather than the complete world-action joint.

results.setting: One history, two actions, utility U=Y. Demonstrations always select action 0 with outcome 1/2. Action 1 gives deterministic outcome 1 in M+ and 0 in M−.
results.metric: Worst-case regret across the two environments
results.value: Proved: every observational learner has regret at least 1/4; exact behavior cloning and world-action imitation have worst-case regret 1/2.
results.comparison: One intervention selecting action 1 identifies the environment and permits zero regret.
results.interpretation: For p=P(A=1), the two regrets are (1-p)/2 and p/2. The separation follows from indistinguishable observational evidence, not greater external policy expressivity. These are analytical values, not robot success rates.

limitations.text: Unrestricted-kernel equivalence does not imply equal expressivity or efficiency at fixed parameter count, memory, latency, or compute. A restricted direct class need not contain the marginal policy represented by a world-action factorization.

Matching p_mu(A|H) need not reproduce demonstrations when the demonstrator uses omitted private information. Appendix B.2 explains how marginalization destroys action dependence on the hidden variable.

The approximate bound demands coverage of deployment histories. Good observational fit alone does not establish that premise, particularly when planning reaches histories or selects actions outside behavior support.

The one-intervention result relies on a deterministic distinguishing outcome. It provides no intervention sample-complexity guarantee for noisy or high-dimensional environments, and the paper supplies no empirical benchmark or mechanism ablation.

A future representation must retain information relevant to utility and subsequent decisions. The arbitrary future-label formulation should not be read as guaranteeing that a visually accurate video predictor is sufficient for sequential planning.

reproduction.text: A minimal verification can enumerate Appendix A.8's two environments, compute both regret functions over action probability p, and verify the observational lower bound and intervention-based policy choices. This checks the constructive theorem rather than reproducing a learned robotics system.

A mechanism test should hold an exact, supported, unconfounded future-action joint fixed and compare ordinary marginalization with action-clamped utility maximization. Removing support or introducing Appendix A.7's hidden variable would separately test the identification assumptions.

A neural extension would require choices absent from this formal comparison: architectures, finite datasets and splits, optimizers, utility-relevant future representations, and evaluation of action effects. Repository availability was not checked; no code was inspected and no experiments were run.

reasoning.text: The recorded foundational/theory and classical world-model/model-based-RL placement fits a paper comparing abstract controller classes, identification conditions, and planning objectives. Architecture and prediction quadrants are not applicable to the work as a whole: it analyzes several mechanisms without proposing a particular network. Allowing a single-network joint does not establish a concrete One Model architecture.

discussionQuestions: With a fixed learned joint, how much utility improvement comes specifically from action-clamped planning, and how does imperfect causal identification affect it? [E13, E14]
Under matched parameter and inference-compute budgets, which policies can a world-action factorization represent more efficiently than direct prediction? [E21]
How does the deterministic intervention advantage change when outcomes are noisy and action coverage must be acquired at a cost? [E17]

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title page and arXiv version line
evidence.detail: The supplied title and identifier match the catalog. The author is Yang Yu, consistent with the catalog's surname-first form. The observed version is arXiv:2608.22197v1, dated 23 August 2026.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 2–4, Section 1, paradigm descriptions, four comparison questions, and main results
evidence.detail: The introduction separates expressivity, population targets, identification, and learning error; it focuses on the first three and contrasts behavior reproduction with action comparison.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6–8, Sections 3.1–3.3, Eqs. (1)–(7), Definitions 3.1–3.4
evidence.detail: Defines the partially observed process, common history, future labels, population risk, trajectory-based capability classes, and observational versus interventional learner inputs.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 8–9, Section 3.4, Assumptions 3.5 and 3.6
evidence.detail: Equivalence assumes common deployment information and observational data, realizability, exact population optimization, and distribution-preserving deployment. Demonstrator trajectory equality additionally requires actions to depend only on the recorded history.
Specifies direct and world-action likelihood objectives, the future/inverse joint factorization, and marginal deployment. A single network is included if its joint admits these conditionals.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 10–11, Section 3.5.3, Eqs. (16)–(20), and Table 1
evidence.detail: Defines interventional outcome and next-history kernels, one-step expected utility, sequential model rollouts, and policy optimization. Table 1 contrasts these operations with observational action reproduction.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 11–12, Sections 4.1–4.2, Proposition 4.3 and Theorem 4.4, Eqs. (21)–(27); Appendix A.1–A.2, p. 21
evidence.detail: Decision-complete control distance equals trajectory TV. Marginalizing a world-action controller yields an identical external action kernel; a point-mass future gives the converse unrestricted representation.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 12–13, Section 4.3, Theorem 4.6, Eqs. (28)–(30), Remark 4.7; Appendix A.3, pp. 21–22
evidence.detail: Likelihood decomposition identifies exact observational conditionals. Marginalizing them recovers the behavior-action conditional; behavior sufficiency supports trajectory equality. Modified future selection is outside this population-action equality.

evidence.location: PDF p. 13, Section 4.4, Proposition 4.8, Eqs. (31)–(35); Appendix A.4, p. 22
evidence.detail: Component TV errors bound action disagreement by their clipped sum. Uniform validity on reachable histories yields the trajectory bound 1-(1-epsilon)^T, at most T epsilon, through coupling.

evidence.location: PDF p. 14, Section 4.5, Eqs. (36)–(37) and following discussion
evidence.detail: Conditioning on recorded futures reduces Bayes action-prediction risk. The author discusses possible representation, pretraining, and transfer benefits while noting that deployment must predict the unavailable future.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 14–15, Section 5.1, Eqs. (38)–(41)
evidence.detail: Under temporary causal identification, the future predictor is a behavior-weighted outcome mixture, and the inverse conditional combines action effects with the behavior action prior.

evidence.location: PDF p. 15, Section 5.2, Theorem 5.1, Eqs. (42)–(47); Appendix A.5, p. 23
evidence.detail: Interventional KL risk decomposes into conditional action-outcome mutual information and divergence from the candidate-action mixture. The mixture minimizes action-unconditioned risk; an exact action-conditioned model has zero risk.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 16–17, Section 5.3, Proposition 5.2, Eqs. (48)–(57); Appendix A.6, p. 23
evidence.detail: Normalizing an exact joint at a supported action recovers its observational forward conditional. Consistency, conditional exchangeability, and positivity identify that conditional as an interventional outcome distribution.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 17–18, Section 5.3, Eqs. (58)–(61) and Corollary 5.3
evidence.detail: The same joint recovers behavior under marginal deployment or supports true one-step utility maximization when identified action-conditioned outcomes are explicitly compared.

evidence.location: PDF p. 18, Section 5.4, Theorem 5.4; Appendix A.7, pp. 23–24
evidence.detail: Separate constructions show non-identification from unsupported actions and hidden confounding. In the confounded example, A=Z makes Y=A and Y=Z observationally identical despite differing intervention outcomes.

evidence.location: PDF p. 18, Section 5.5, Eqs. (62)–(64), Corollary 5.5
evidence.detail: With an exact interventional next-history model throughout candidate-policy reachability and exact optimization, model-based control exceeds exact imitation by the demonstrator's suboptimality gap.

evidence.location: PDF p. 19, Theorem 5.6; Appendix A.8, p. 25, potential-outcome table and regret derivation
evidence.detail: Both environments demonstrate action 0 with outcome 1/2. Action 1 yields 1 or 0. For action-1 probability p, regrets are (1-p)/2 and p/2, proving the 1/4 observational lower bound, 1/2 exact-imitation worst case, and zero regret after one distinguishing intervention.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 19–20, Section 6, especially the explicit limitations on p. 20
evidence.detail: The conclusion limits claims to class-level and population analysis, disclaims statistical and optimization guarantees, and discusses deployment information, decoding, causal identification, and utility-relevant future representations.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 25–26, Appendix B.1, Point decoding
evidence.detail: The example contrasts distributional deployment with MAP future selection, which changes the action marginal. Conditional-mean decoding can preserve an expectation without preserving the full action distribution.

evidence.location: PDF p. 26, Appendix B.2–B.3
evidence.detail: An independently sampled action with the correct observed marginal need not preserve dependence on a demonstrator-only variable. The marginalization identity also extends to action chunks and common language conditioning.

evidence.location: PDF p. 27, Appendix B.4–B.5
evidence.detail: Restricted direct classes require closure under marginalization to represent all corresponding world-action policies. Identification on behavior support does not ensure accuracy at actions or histories selected by an optimized policy.
